perspective:
I am Sara Manuelito, a Speech-Language Pathologist. Shirley Whiteplume is my long-time nurse colleague and close friend; we have worked together at a community health center for several years.

- We shared care for a mutual patient who died, and I attended his funeral with Shirley. There I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected she was deeply affected.
- I told Shirley I knew this must be hard and that I had seen how much she cared for him. She said it had been tough and she kept thinking if more could have been done.
- I said we did everything we could and should remember the good care and moments of joy we brought him. Shirley said it was hard to let go.
- Later, during a coffee break at work, I brought up our treatment decisions, sensing Shirley might feel burdened. She said she felt responsible and wondered if pushing for a different approach might have helped.
- I said we made the best decisions with the information we had, and it was too heavy a burden to carry alone. Shirley appreciated it but said accepting it was hard.
- I observed Shirley continuing to be reserved and minimally expressive. In a quiet moment in our office, I told her I noticed she was holding back feelings and it was okay to be open.
- Shirley said she was not sure she could and did not want to seem unprofessional or weak. I said showing emotion does not make her weak. She said maybe I was right and she would try to be more open.
- I later felt my confrontation might have been too harsh, so I apologized for coming on too strong. Shirley said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated the apology. I said I was there for her. She thanked me and said we should keep talking; it helps.
- After some time, I noticed improvements in Shirley’s demeanor and felt hopeful. I asked how she was feeling. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support.
- I suggested spending more time together outside work. Shirley said she would like that and suggested planning something for the weekend.
